passage:
On a Saturday morning, Lina and her friend Tariq help plan a short community walk in the fictional town of Glenford. They want everyone to understand the route before setting off, including visitors who have never been there. The group will meet beside the library at nine. Someone from the walking club will bring a paper map, and Lina will bring a compass. Neither item replaces local signs or advice; the group will ask the park staff if anything is unclear.

From the library, people should use the sidewalk along the main street until they reach the first junction. The sidewalk is the space for people on foot; the dark pavement beside it is the paved surface used by vehicles. At the intersection, a clock on a tall building is an easy landmark. The guide asks everyone to wait there and check that the whole group has arrived. The club also plans a short rest for anyone who needs one. From the clock they will go east toward a bridge over a stream. They will not enter the old tunnel nearby because the park has closed it for maintenance.

Beyond the bridge is a field with a low fence. A broad path follows the water for a while and then turns south into a meadow. In spring the meadow has flowers, and the group can stop without leaving the marked trail. Tariq points to a hill on the west side of the valley. Its lower slope is gentle, but the upper part is steep and can be slippery after rain. Lina does not plan to climb the hill; she wants a walk that the whole group has agreed is comfortable.

The guide checks the latest local notice before Saturday. It says that the narrow path beside the stream can become muddy. If that path is closed, the walkers will follow a wider track through the field instead. The notice also shows a covered shelter beside the visitor center. This is the second meeting place, not a place to wait alone. If someone becomes separated, they should contact the guide using the number printed on the group note. Nobody needs to guess a direction or hurry to catch up.

On the practice walk, Tariq asks what the word “it” means in their written directions. In the sentence about the tunnel, it refers to the tunnel, not the bridge. They change another sentence so that the name of the path appears instead of an unclear “this.” At the end of the route they descend a short slope back toward the visitor center. Lina sends everyone the two meeting places and a simple reminder to check the park's current information. The story is a language exercise, so real groups should use their own local guidance.
